dedupe_keys.name: climate change hotspots for the global subsea telecommunications network 2022

description: This risk assessment reviews how climate change will affect the subsea cables that carry more than 95 per cent of international data, and their landing stations and shore-side plant. Led by Michael Clare of the UK National Oceanography Centre with co-authors from the University of Southampton, the University of Central Florida, the US Geological Survey, New Zealand and the International Cable Protection Committee, the study synthesised published datasets on hazards to cables, such as tropical cyclones, river floods that trigger seabed turbidity currents, sea level rise, coastal erosion, changing ocean currents and ice melt, and on where cables run. It identified hotspots where impacts are likely to be greatest, noting that not all regions will be affected in the same way or at the same time; examples include the waters off Taiwan, where stronger typhoons and river floods already break cables, the polar regions, where ice and ocean conditions are changing fastest, and low-lying landing sites exposed to sea level rise and erosion. It warns that single events can damage several cable systems at once and isolate whole regions, and calls for route planning, monitoring and landing-site adaptation. Coverage: global cable network, projections through this century. Format and access: Earth-Science Reviews article, with an accepted version on the NERC Open Research Archive; free copy. Caveats: a synthesis, not a quantitative probabilistic model; cable locations are generalised. Simulation uses: hazard exposure of submarine cables and landing stations, adaptation planning of routes and landing sites, and network resilience to regional isolation. Related records: the TeleGeography submarine cable map gives routes, and the Tonga cable cut of 2022 is an example.
